{{Short description|Operation on a knot producing a link with two components}}

[[File:Bing double of unknot.svg|thumb|The [[unknot]] (left) and its Bing double (right).]]

In [[knot theory]], a field of [[mathematics]], the '''Bing double''' of a knot is a link with two components which follow the pattern of the knot and "hook together". Bing doubles were introduced in {{harvtxt|Bing|1952}} by their namesake, the American mathematician [[R. H. Bing]].{{sfn|Cimasoni|2006|p=2395}} The Bing double of a [[slice knot]] is a [[slice link]], though it is unknown whether the converse is true.{{sfn|Cimasoni|2006|p=2397}} The components of a Bing double bound disjoint [[Seifert surface]]s.{{sfn|Cimasoni|2006|p=2397}}

[[File:Solid torus surrounding Bing double of unknot.svg|thumb|A [[solid torus]] encasing the Bing double of the unknot. ]]

The Bing double of a knot {{math|''K''}} is defined by placing the Bing double of the unknot in the [[solid torus]] surrounding it, as shown in the figure, and then twisting that solid torus into the shape of {{math|''K''}}.{{sfn|Cimasoni|2006|p=2397}} This definition is similar to that for [[Whitehead double]]s. The Bing double of the unknot is also called the '''Bing link'''.{{sfn|Jiang|Lin|Wang|Wu|2002|pp=189-190}}
